author: A Robot
objectives: Identify DNA structural components: sugar-phosphate backbones, nitrogenous bases, and hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs.
Apply complementary base-pairing rules and relate A-T versus G-C pairing to molecular fit and hydrogen-bond count.
Explain antiparallel DNA strand orientation using 5' to 3' sugar-phosphate backbone directionality.
Trace helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase functions at the replication fork.
Explain continuous leading-strand synthesis and discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis as consequences of antiparallel templates and 5' to 3' polymerase activity.
Describe semiconservative replication and predict daughter DNA strand composition after one and two replication rounds.

modules.description: Students inspect a 3D DNA helix and reveal the backbone, bases, and hydrogen bonds that stabilize complementary base pairs.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the two sugar-phosphate backbones and internal nitrogenous base pairs in a DNA double helix.
Describe the spatial organization of bases projecting inward between the backbones.
Distinguish A-T base pairs with two hydrogen bonds from G-C base pairs with three hydrogen bonds.
instructions: Place the model on a tabletop about half a meter in front of you.
Use Next to reveal each structural feature.
Compare the two highlighted base pairs and their hydrogen-bond markers.

components.text: Two backbones outside; bases pair inside
DNA: two strands twisted into a double helix

clips.changeMeaning: The full DNA double helix is centered in the workspace so students can perceive the molecule as a three-dimensional spiral rather than a flat ladder.
clips.narration: DNA is a double helix: two long strands twist around a shared central axis. The outside rails represent sugar-phosphate backbones, while the rungs inside represent paired nitrogenous bases.

components.text: Sugar-phosphate backbones spiral on the outside

clips.changeMeaning: The two spiral backbone highlights are enabled to isolate the sugar-phosphate strands from the internal base pairs.
clips.narration: Each strand has a repeating sugar-phosphate backbone. These backbones form the outside of the helix and provide directionality because each sugar has chemically distinct five-prime and three-prime ends.

components.text: Bases project inward: A, T, G, and C

clips.changeMeaning: Representative A-T and G-C base-pair objects appear through the center of the helix to emphasize inward-facing complementary bases.
clips.narration: The four nitrogenous bases are adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine. They project inward from the two backbones and pair across the helix, creating the rungs of the twisted ladder.

components.text: A–T: 2 H bonds     G–C: 3 H bonds

clips.changeMeaning: Hydrogen bond dash markers appear over the base pairs, with two dashes for A-T and three dashes for G-C.
clips.narration: Complementary base pairing is specific: adenine pairs with thymine using two hydrogen bonds, while guanine pairs with cytosine using three hydrogen bonds. These pairings maintain a uniform helix width.

modules.description: A straightened DNA segment reveals opposite 5' and 3' orientations and connects directionality to complementary sequence reading.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain what 5' and 3' labels mean for DNA strand directionality at an introductory molecular level.
Describe why complementary DNA strands run antiparallel.
Use a short template sequence to infer the complementary sequence and its orientation.
instructions: Inspect the two straightened DNA strands.
Follow the arrows and endpoint labels as they appear.
Use the displayed sequence to practice complementary pairing.

components.text: Untwisted view of paired DNA strands

clips.changeMeaning: The helix is represented as two straightened strands so directionality can be shown clearly with labels and arrows.
clips.narration: To understand directionality, it helps to untwist a small region of the helix. The two sugar-phosphate backbones are not oriented the same way; they run in opposite directions.

clips.changeMeaning: 5' and 3' endpoint labels appear on opposite ends of each strand, showing reversed orientation between strands.
clips.narration: One strand runs five-prime to three-prime from left to right. The complementary strand runs three-prime to five-prime from left to right. This opposite orientation is called antiparallel.

components.text:
5'- A G T C -3'
3'- T C A G -5'

clips.changeMeaning: The sequence label changes from a single template to a paired sequence, reinforcing complementary pairing and orientation.
clips.narration: If the top strand is five-prime A G T C three-prime, the complementary strand must be three-prime T C A G five-prime. The bases pair A with T and G with C, but the strand directions remain opposite.

modules.description: A dynamic replication fork scene demonstrates helicase unwinding, SSB protein stabilization, and DNA polymerase extension.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify helicase, single-strand binding proteins, and DNA polymerase at a replication fork.
Describe how helicase separates parental strands and how SSB proteins stabilize exposed single strands.
Explain that DNA polymerase extends only from a 3' end and synthesizes DNA in the 5' to 3' direction.
instructions: Watch the replication fork open in stages.
Track each enzyme by its label and color.
Notice the direction DNA polymerase moves relative to each template.

components.text: Parental strands form a replication fork

clips.changeMeaning: A Y-shaped parental DNA fork appears to establish the replication fork workspace before enzymes are introduced.
clips.narration: DNA replication begins where the double helix opens. The Y-shaped structure shown here is a replication fork, with parental template strands separating from each other.

components.text: Helicase unwinds the parental double helix

clips.changeMeaning: The helicase enzyme appears at the fork junction and shifts forward, indicating active unwinding of the helix.
clips.narration: Helicase unwinds the double helix by disrupting hydrogen bonds between paired bases. As helicase moves, the fork opens and exposes single-stranded templates.

clips.changeMeaning: Single-strand binding proteins appear along both separated templates to show stabilization of exposed single-stranded DNA.
clips.narration: Single-strand binding proteins bind to the exposed parental strands. They keep the strands from reannealing or forming secondary structures before DNA polymerase copies them.

clips.changeMeaning: DNA polymerase enzymes and red nascent DNA segments appear on both templates to introduce 5' to 3' synthesis.
clips.narration: DNA polymerase synthesizes new DNA by adding nucleotides to a three-prime hydroxyl end. This means every new strand is extended in the five-prime to three-prime direction.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Leading and Lagging Strand Synthesis
modules.description: Students compare continuous leading-strand synthesis to discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis, including Okazaki fragments and ligase.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare continuous leading-strand synthesis with discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis.
Relate Okazaki fragment formation to DNA polymerase's 5' to 3' synthesis constraint.
Describe DNA ligase's role in sealing nicks between Okazaki fragments.
instructions: Follow the moving fork from left to right.
Compare the long continuous red strand to separated red Okazaki fragments.
Observe how ligase joins fragments into a continuous strand.

components.text: Fork movement plus antiparallel templates creates asymmetry

clips.changeMeaning: The fork and fork-direction arrow establish that both templates are copied while the fork advances in one direction.
clips.narration: At each replication fork, both parental templates must be copied. The fork advances in one direction, but the two templates are antiparallel, so DNA polymerase cannot copy both in exactly the same way.

clips.changeMeaning: The leading polymerase and continuous leading strand extend toward the fork, showing continuous synthesis in the same general direction as fork opening.
clips.narration: On the leading-strand template, DNA polymerase can synthesize continuously in the same direction that the fork opens. The growing daughter strand extends five-prime to three-prime as polymerase follows the fork.

clips.changeMeaning: Multiple separated Okazaki fragments appear on the lagging template to show discontinuous synthesis away from the fork in short segments.
clips.narration: On the lagging-strand template, DNA polymerase still synthesizes five-prime to three-prime, but this direction points away from the moving fork. The result is discontinuous synthesis in short Okazaki fragments.

components.text: DNA ligase seals fragments into one strand

clips.changeMeaning: Ligase appears, and Okazaki fragments are replaced by a continuous sealed strand to show the final joining step.
clips.narration: DNA ligase seals the remaining nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone between Okazaki fragments. After ligase acts, the lagging daughter strand becomes continuous.

modules.description: A concluding product scene shows parental and daughter DNA molecules, emphasizing that each daughter contains one original and one newly synthesized strand.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define semiconservative replication using daughter DNA composition.
Identify original parental strands versus newly synthesized strands in daughter molecules.
Predict strand composition after one and two rounds of DNA replication.
instructions: Compare blue parental strands with red newly synthesized strands.
Step through one replication round and then a second-round prediction.
Use the final labels to summarize semiconservative inheritance.

components.text: Blue = parental strand; Red = new strand
Start: both strands are parental blue

clips.changeMeaning: A single all-parental DNA molecule is staged as the starting point for semiconservative replication.
clips.narration: Before replication, this DNA molecule contains two parental strands. In this scene, parental strands are colored blue, while newly synthesized strands are colored red.

clips.changeMeaning: Two hybrid daughter DNA molecules appear and the parent molecule moves upward slightly, showing that each daughter contains one parental and one new strand.
clips.narration: After one round of replication, two daughter DNA molecules are produced. Each daughter has one original parental strand and one newly synthesized strand. That is why DNA replication is called semiconservative.

clips.changeMeaning: Four second-round products appear with two hybrid and two all-new molecules, helping students predict strand composition after repeated replication.
clips.narration: If those daughters replicate again, each original blue strand remains paired with a new red strand in one molecule, while the red strands from round one template additional red strands. After two rounds, two molecules still contain one original strand, and two contain only strands made after the start.

components.text: Complementarity + antiparallel strands drive DNA replication

clips.changeMeaning: The final label changes to a concise concept map summarizing how DNA structure determines replication mechanism and semiconservative products.
clips.narration: DNA structure explains replication. Complementary bases allow accurate copying. Antiparallel backbones force leading and lagging synthesis. Semiconservative replication preserves one parental strand in each daughter molecule after the first round.
